1.pericope_label: The hand of the Lord was upon me, and carried me out in the spirit of the Lord, and set me down in the midst of the valley which was full of bones, And caused me to pass by them round about: and, behold, there were very many in the open valley; and, lo, they were very dry. And he said unto me, Son of man, can these bones live? And I answered, O Lord God, thou knowest. Again he said unto me, Prophesy upon these bones, and say unto them, O ye dry bones, hear the word of the Lord. Thus saith the Lord God unto these bones; Behold, I will cause breath to enter into you, and ye shall live: And I will lay sinews upon you, and will bring up flesh upon you, and cover you with skin, and put breath in you, and ye shall live; and ye shall know that I am the Lord. So I prophesied as I was commanded: and as I prophesied, there was a noise, and behold a shaking, and the bones came together, bone to his bone. And when I beheld, lo, the sinews and the flesh came up upon them, and the skin covered them above: but there was no breath in them. Then said he unto me, Prophesy unto the wind, prophesy, son of man, and say to the wind, Thus saith the Lord God; Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe upon these slain, that they may live. So I prophesied as he commanded me, and the breath came into them, and they lived, and stood up upon their feet, an exceeding great army. Then he said unto me, Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel: behold, they say, Our bones are dried, and our hope is lost: we are cut off for our parts. Therefore prophesy and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord God; Behold, O my people, I will open your graves, and cause you to come up out of your graves, and bring you into the land of Israel. And ye shall know that I am the Lord, when I have opened your graves, O my people, and brought you up out of your graves, And shall put my spirit in you, and ye shall live, and I shall place you in your own land: then shall ye know that I the Lord have spoken it, and performed it, saith the Lord.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch divide the chapter into two revelations, a vision of resurrection and an acted sign of reunion; Ellicott places the scene in the plain of the earlier visions since the word carries the article, repunctuates so that the bones become a fresh statement rather than a description, takes the dryness for a measure of how long life had gone, says the question presses a human impossibility that omnipotence is about to overturn at once and was the lesson needed by hearers who had disbelieved threats and now disbelieved promises, notes that prophesying here means speaking on God's behalf without any idea of prediction, observes that one Hebrew word carries breath, wind and spirit alike, makes the two stages of the restoration an echo of the creation account, marks the dead as specifically the slain, and corrects an obscure clause to read that as for us, we are cut off.

Gill turns the question into a fruitless search for means, has sinews laid first to join and then flesh to cover and give motion, marks the two prophesyings as distinct with the first leaving the work unfinished for want of breath, and lists what the promised Spirit works in those who receive it.

Clarke summarises the chapter as a scattered people's hopeless condition reversed against all probability, counts six stages from bones through ligaments, muscle and skin to bodies complete but soulless and then the entering breath, compares the first man before he received his own principle of life, reads the summons to the four winds as a call to souls from every quarter, equates bones with condition and revival with return, calls the graves a pointed allusion to a resurrection the people already believed, and distinguishes the soul already given from the Spirit that makes men obedient; Wesley finds three resurrections in the figure, souls out of the death of sin, a church out of affliction into liberty, and the body at the last day, and dwells on the noise, a rattling and a commotion large enough to declare a presence, then a gliding together in which not one bone of all those slain was missing or misplaced.

Henry insists the thing shown is beyond nature, since there is no road back from deprivation to possession, so that only a word from God could suggest it, and reports the argument that the vision could not confirm anything unless the general resurrection it borrows were itself certain.

debates.question: What does the word rendered breath mean here?

positions.position: Soul, though the term also covers breath, wind and sometimes the Spirit of God.
One Hebrew word carries breath, wind and spirit alike, and only the context can decide.
The soul, whose emblem here is wind.

outliers.claim: Dwells on the reassembly, in which of all the bones of all those slain not one was missing, none went astray and none took a wrong place, offering it as a picture of scattered atoms gathered at the last.
Suggests that a mind long occupied with devastating campaigns would come by the image of a plain strewn with bones naturally enough.

15.pericope_label: The word of the Lord came again unto me, saying, Moreover, thou son of man, take thee one stick, and write upon it, For Judah, and for the children of Israel his companions: then take another stick, and write upon it, For Joseph, the stick of Ephraim, and for all the house of Israel his companions: And join them one to another into one stick; and they shall become one in thine hand. And when the children of thy people shall speak unto thee, saying, Wilt thou not shew us what thou meanest by these? Say unto them, Thus saith the Lord God; Behold, I will take the stick of Joseph, which is in the hand of Ephraim, and the tribes of Israel his fellows, and will put them with him, even with the stick of Judah, and make them one stick, and they shall be one in mine hand. And the sticks whereon thou writest shall be in thine hand before their eyes. And say unto them, Thus saith the Lord God; Behold, I will take the children of Israel from among the heathen, whither they be gone, and will gather them on every side, and bring them into their own land: And I will make them one nation in the land upon the mountains of Israel; and one king shall be king to them all: and they shall be no more two nations, neither shall they be divided into two kingdoms any more at all: Neither shall they defile themselves any more with their idols, nor with their detestable things, nor with any of their transgressions: but I will save them out of all their dwellingplaces, wherein they have sinned, and will cleanse them: so shall they be my people, and I will be their God. And David my servant shall be king over them; and they all shall have one shepherd: they shall also walk in my judgments, and observe my statutes, and do them. And they shall dwell in the land that I have given unto Jacob my servant, wherein your fathers have dwelt; and they shall dwell therein, even they, and their children, and their children’s children for ever: and my servant David shall be their prince for ever. Moreover I will make a covenant of peace with them; it shall be an everlasting covenant with them: and I will place them, and multiply them, and will set my sanctuary in the midst of them for evermore. My tabernacle also shall be with them: yea, I will be their God, and they shall be my people. And the heathen shall know that I the Lord do sanctify Israel, when my sanctuary shall be in the midst of them for evermore.

schools.summary: Ellicott denies that these are the rods of the earlier trial of the tribes since the word differs and means simply a piece of wood, supposes the two shaped to look like one when held together, explains why neither kingdom could be named alone, sets the human hand that made the division against the hand in which the pieces become one, notes that the joined wood was to stay in the prophet's hand while the promise was explained, holds that the gathering was fulfilled to a remnant only with any larger fulfilment prevented by the people's sins, points out how heavily the text leans on for ever, and traces the promised tabernacle from a shadow in the rebuilt temple to an incarnation the Greek describes with the same verb.

Gill offers tablet, board or plank for the object and takes it as an emblem of a kingdom, reports the Jewish commentators who make the promised king the Messiah of whom the older king was a type, takes the covenant of peace for the covenant of grace with reconciliation as its principal article and the tabernacle for an indwelling that makes each of them a temple, and closes on the watching nations who are to observe what holiness God works in a people set apart.

Clarke sets out the composition of the two states and notes that some individuals rejoined the south without altering the division, observes that the distinction did disappear after the return while denying that a single king ever followed politically so that the union belongs to another time and kingdom, and identifies the tabernacle with Christ himself; Wesley calls the object a writing tablet or tally, identifies the companions on each side, reads the earlier united reign as a type and finds the peace-maker in the name of the king who followed it, and takes the sanctuary for a spiritual temple never abolished on earth and consummated in heaven.
Henry states the promise as brotherly union ending feuds that ran from the first revolt, and reads through it to a wider peace under the Messiah.

debates.question: How far does the promise of one king over one nation reach?

positions.position: Not to the return: the distinction between the kingdoms did vanish, but no single king followed politically, so the union belongs to another kingdom.
To the Messiah directly, the earlier united reign being a type and the peace-maker named in the king who followed it.
The gathering was the first step but fulfilled to a remnant only, any larger fulfilment being prevented by the people's own sins.

outliers.claim: Distinguishes these pieces of wood from the rods of the earlier trial of the tribes, and supposes them shaped so that when held together they would appear as one.
Concedes that the two kingdoms ceased to be distinguished after the return while denying that any single king followed, so that the promised union must belong elsewhere.
